utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you. This is the 12th day of June, 2007. I greet everyone from the Prosecution, Defence counsel, and the accused and all others. As you know, I noticed the parties this morning that we will stop at 5.30 -- 5.25 tonight, this afternoon because there's a Plenary Session at 5.30 for Judges, and this Plenary has to do with administrative matters of this Tribunal and all Judges need to be there. So we will shorten this hearing by an hour. Since we gave six hours to Defence altogether for the two and a half hours -- two and a half days to come, Defence will have plenty of time for their cross. Prosecution has already spent one hour and 35 minutes. Ideally, it would be best if you stop before the break we'll have for this hearing. Ms. Gillett, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, you recall yesterday evening just before we adjourned for the evening I was trying to clarify a particular matter with you and I would like to revisit that matter now.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could Mr. Buljko be provided with the -- with his statements and the binder as well from yesterday, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Buljko, your statements that are not in the binder, they're in front of you. If you could turn to your statement from the year 2000, which is numbered Exhibit 10069. And if you turn to page 11 in the English or page 18 in the B/C/S, whichever you'd prefer to look at. For my purposes, starting on page 11 of the English, you state that you were a member of the ABiH delegation negotiating with the HVO to allow the first humanitarian aid convoy to enter East Mostar since the beginning of the conflict in Mostar between the HVO and the ABiH in May 1993. Now, what I would like to ask you in relation to that specific part of the statement, where did that meeting that you attended, where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting took place in East Mostar, in premises there. It was just a delegation of the BH army and the commission for the exchange, and I said that it was Mr. Sulejman Budakovic and Mr. Alikadic, and the mediator was Mr. Albert Benabou on behalf of the civil police. And on the Croatian side, as far as I remember, I think it was Mr. Thornberry who talked to them on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You said in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Gillett, for interrupting you. I believe it was a technical mistake in the translation. When the witness answered to you, he said according to the transcript, "And on the Croatian side, as far as I remember, I think it was Mr. Thornberry ... " But Mr. Thornberry should have been from the UN side, UNHCR side, et cetera. So I believe that it was a mistake in translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It had confused me somewhat. I was about to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Who did attend for the Croatian side at that particular meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN BULJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On behalf of the Croatian side, I have to say the following: This paragraph is part of a broader statement by me, and I have to tell the Trial Chamber that there's a slight mistake that was made. I was at a meeting led by Mr. Albert Benabou with the representative of the BH army and the commission for the exchanges, and I took notes which I have submitted to the Trial Chamber. Now, as far as the Croatian side is concerned, I think that Mr. Thornberry was the mediator and dealt with the entry of the convoy with them for East Mostar. I know that because Mr. Thornberry wrote a book in which he talks about those difficult negotiations which took place. It's called, "the Peace Forces, Humanitarian Aid, and Conflict." That's a book of his. And he talks about East Mostar and negotiations that were very difficult and that Croatia should be included, Mr. Mate Granic, and then he also speaks about the conditions set for the entry of the first convoy of humanitarian aid. On the 31st of August, that is to say, right after the convoy entered, this humanitarian aid convoy, we had a meeting with Mr. Thornberry, who had as the topic of discussion the evacuation of the wounded, and at that meeting, which was attended by Alija Alikadic, Dr. Milavic, and I think Mr. Humo as well and myself, Mr. Thornberry said that for the evacuation of the wounded, the next day, that is to say, the 1st of September we would have an a meeting in Medjugorje. We asked who with and he said with Bruno Stojic and that the meeting would enable us to implement the agreement. So that is why I said what I said. I said that Mr. Bruno Stojic was the person who at that point in time was involved in the negotiations with the international community with respect to the entry of the humanitarian aid convoy into Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, excuse me, because I see you are on your feet, but I wanted to -- no, you have the floor. You have the floor. I just wanted the witness to continue and finish with his speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Your Honour, I think the time has come, with all due respect, when the Trial Chamber should intervene and ask this witness directly, reminding him that he has stated under oath that he was present at a meeting of all the parties, to challenge him as to whether he was actually present at such a meeting, and to find out who was present. We've now been discussing this for a considerable time, and I think it's very obvious that this witness has not yet volunteered the truth on this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were under oath, you made a solemn declaration saying that you would only tell the truth, and of course, there are duties, and in case of perjury you could be prosecuted. But this is not the question. What you're saying might be -- is probably the truth, but there are things that are not very specific, and imprecise. When you said you attended a meeting, it means that you were there. Then when you mention the fact that Mr. Bruno Stojic was at a meeting, does it mean that you were also there and you saw him with your own eyes, or is it something that you actually inferred? Of course, answering questions on things that happened 14 years ago is difficult. Myself, I would -- it would be very difficult for me to say whether I actually attended a meeting, yes or no. And my only -- the only way out would be to look at documents to be sure. So if you're absolutely sure, please say so. If you're not absolutely sure, say that you don't remember, because everything you're saying is noted in the transcript. And later when we will have to rule and make a judgement, we will look at the transcript, and this will probably be an instrument that we use in our decision-making process. So you have to be very specific. If you're absolutely sure that Mr. Stojic was present at a meeting, say so and say -- say why. And if you're not sure, say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I explained a moment ago what the situation was exactly with respect to this, and I said that there was a mistake, and I said it was a paragraph from my statement which probably referred to the talks. And I attended the talks where the mediator was Mr. Albert Benabou with the BH army and the exchange commission. I don't know about the Croatian side. I explained what Mr. Thornberry said on the 31st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you correctly, and I think I have understood you correctly, there was a meeting that you attended. You were present with Mr. Benabou and members of the ABiH. This meeting is devoted on the topic of the convoy and humanitarian aid, but you're also saying that on the Croatian side there must have been some other meeting with Mr. Thornberry. And according to what you're saying, Mr. Stojic may have attended this meeting. And you seem to be drawing this conclusion from the book written by Mr. Thornberry on the matter, but aren't you just mixing up things? Because there's hearsay, what you actually know, and Mr. Thornberry's book. We see that you're using a piece ever paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took notes from all the meetings. The meeting with Mr. Thornberry on the 31st of August was held in East Mostar, and at that meeting Mr. Thornberry said that the next day, that is to say the 1st of September, 1993, a meeting would be held in Medjugorje, and we asked who with, and he said with Mr. Bruno Stojic. I have that written down in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but it seems to me that the witness has those very notes in front of him now. We have not received the notes. I don't know if the Prosecutor has seen them, and I'd like to mention that in the witness statement he didn't say any of this, so it's all new to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These -- this paper that you just took out of your pocket, they're your notes. Did you give them to Prosecution, or does Prosecution not know about them and you've been holding on to these preciously for a number of years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hand them over to the Prosecution. The Prosecution does not know about them. I had these notes -- in fact, I have a lot of those documents that I wasn't able to provide at that time because I probably didn't know but they cropped up recently, I found them quite recently, I saw them. And I have them in the original where it says at that particular meeting the following day, that is to say, in September, that -- that Mr. Bruno Stojic was to meet with Mr. Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, in those notes that you have, there is proof that a meeting was held on August 31st and that the day after, on September 1st, in Medjugorje, there was supposed to be a meeting which should have been attended by Mr. Stojic. Should have been. It's just an assumption. So actually, you don't know whether on September 1st Mr. Stojic actually attended this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether he was. That's the information we received from Mr. Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point it would appear that we would be entitled to these notes, irrespective of whether the Prosecution wishes to see them or not. Obviously, they were not aware of these notes. But now since the gentleman seems to be looking at the notes, at least he must have looked at them overnight. He must have them here. We are entitled to them. And I suggest that until we see them that any further questioning be suspended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you see a problem in giving us your notes? This piece of paper that you were toying with earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want all of his notes, Your Honour, everything, and all the documents that the gentleman has, everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I have is this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not going to ask him for his wallet, Mr. Karnavas, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if there are notes in the wallet, I guess I would. But I find it difficult to believe that he has one sheet of paper that are his notes that just coincidentally answer the very same questions that were being posed to him yesterday. It's rather incredulous. So he must have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir. Sir, this paper, these are the notes that come from the meeting of August 31st?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Do you agree with giving us these -- with disclosing this paper right away to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't mind giving it; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Then we'll take it, and we'll show it to Defence. Usher, would you please get this paper, and we will also like to look at it at the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But I think that the Chamber is seized by a request to hand all the notes over. This must be specified. Mr. Karnavas, I would suggest that you want the notes within the time frame covered by the indictment, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. At least with respect to what the gentleman intends to be testifying about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I think that I would like to have -- I think he needs to produce the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I will disclose these notes. It's two photocopies. Obviously these are handwritten notes. One dates -- bears the date August 31, 1993, there's mentions of names, and it seems that there is what these persons said at the time, the persons who actually took the floor. So we have two documents, but the second sheet is absolutely identical to the first one. So I could give one each, one to Defence, one to Prosecution since it's the same sheet. So one for Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Karnavas, unfortunately, cannot speak B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have my colleague who is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will have to give it to your colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I should point out, Your Honours, and I don't mean to be disputatious although it may seem that way at times, that yesterday we were shown a document by the Prosecution, it was 4479, where the gentleman appears to have provided notes to the Prosecution and it would appear that were in his own handwriting. Now today he says that he just came across these notes recently. And I find it hard to believe that that is the case. But assuming that is the case, we have a copy here of one particular page. It would appear that, at least when you're looking at it, there are some lines so it must have been from a notebook. So the only logical conclusion that I can come up with is that perhaps the gentleman before coming here today, while he was at his hotel or someplace else, made copies of this particular sheet of -- made a copy of one -- one page from his notes. And then if I were to put two and two together, it would seem to me that his notebook would be with him, perhaps with his possessions here in The Hague. So, one, I would like the Trial Chamber to ask if that is the case. If indeed that is the case, I certainly would like, and I'm moving for that notebook and any other notes that he may have or any other papers that he may have that might be relevant, because I now question the gentleman's integrity and his credibility as a witness. So that's why I think it's necessary for us to look at, and I think we may need some time to examine them. I don't know whether the Prosecution wishes to go forward with their direct, but at least before doing any cross, we may, we may, need some time. But I'm asking for his notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would join in that -- in that motion. I reserve any -- any comment at this time on the credibility of the witness, but I do join Mr. Karnavas's motion. I think we are entitled to see whatever documents the witness may have that are relevant to the indictment which have not so far been produced before we cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just for the record, my Defence would like to join in the request. It is an official request. We don't always have to have the same opinion, but I consider that the notes that the witness had and used must be disclosed regardless whether they've been disclosed to the Prosecution or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to say one sentence, not to get lost in everything that has gone by. I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber to bear in mind that the statement by the gentleman, which was supposed to be tendered under 92 ter, was provided on the 16th of May and the 10th and 11th of June and in July 2000. Now, in that statement the witness mentions Bruno Stojic linked to the meeting and negotiations with respect to the entry of the convoy on the 24th or, rather, 25th of August. Now, the gentleman said expressly that he -- that Bruno Stojic did attend some of those meetings and gave the okay for the convoys to enter. Now he's telling us about a meeting held on the 31st of August where he indirectly learnt that Mr. Thornberry would be having a meeting with Mr. Bruno Stojic. Now, I should like for the record to draw your attention, to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that this gentleman, after having made the statement, made two other statements and had a meeting with the Prosecutor before these proceedings in court here. At no point did this same gentleman put right what he thought might have been a mistake where he says that he learnt about and knew that Bruno Stojic was at that meeting. He didn't correct that at all. So let's just put aside the meeting of the 31st of August, which in the light of these events with respect to the convoy is not essential. He talked about a meeting on the 30th of August or 31st of August, but did not make any mention of names there, whereas with the other proposals I'd like to join in my colleagues. But for the record, I'd like to state what I just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir -- I will give you the floor in a minute, Mr. Scott, to try not to waste time. So, Witness, the document that you gave us earlier, one sheet of which is with Prosecution and the other sheet with the Defence, I'd like to know whether this sheet comes from a whole notebook, whether it's just a single sheet that you kept with you. So is it a notebook or just one sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a notebook which stayed behind. I wasn't able to provide it to the Tribunal because I didn't have it in my possession. I found it later on. And it is there that the notes are to be found from some of the meetings that were held in East Mostar and possibly somewhere in Medjugorje during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So this notebook, is it in your hotel and you only brought with you one sheet of paper, or do you have here in the Tribunal the entire notebook with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I have the notebook with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have the notebook with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on me. Not on me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left it -- well, I can bring it to you quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where do you leave it, in the hotel, at the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next door. It's obviously next door. Second question: When you met with the Prosecutor, did you talk about this notebook with him? Did you show him the notebook, or did you just stay silent about it? When you met with the Prosecutor before the hearing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, but I didn't think that they needed the notebook. But when I looked through it more carefully and saw what it contained, then last night I sat down and dealt with this and saw that it had quite a number of elements which had to do with all these issues. But, no, I did not manage to read it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica mentioned earlier that in your statement at page 11, when you're talking about the meeting, you say: "On August 24, 1993, I was a member of the ABiH delegation," et cetera, but there is no mention whatsoever of the meeting of August 31st, 1993, in your written statement. When you saw the Prosecutor and the Prosecutor showed you this statement, why didn't you make a correction then, saying this paragraph was ambiguous, because on August 31st there had been a meeting, a meeting that you attended? Because when we see that document, that sheet of paper, you are actually writing down what people that were attending this meeting said. So why didn't you make a correction telling the Prosecutor what is written on page 11 is not really exact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I gave a lengthy statement, Your Honour, I was not able to look at each and every sentence to review it when I met with the Prosecution. And I really do apologise, and a moment ago I explained that there was a misunderstanding, and I explained why this occurred. I told you that I didn't have the notebook at the time, that is to say when I had a meeting with the Prosecution, but that I subsequently found it quite recently, and I just read it last night because I was intrigued to see what it said -- or, rather, I was intrigued by yesterday's discussion concerning Mr. Stojic, and I know that he was mentioned, and that is why in my statements I mentioned Mr. Stojic, saying that he was asked about the entry of the humanitarian aid convoy and now we see about the evacuation of the sick and wounded as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to intervene once again to test the credibility of this witness. The witness said today during the day so far that on the 31st, as we can see on the piece of paper, those of us who can understand the language, we can read it, he had a meeting and that Mr. Thornberry told him that the next day he would have a meeting with Mr. Stojic to discuss the wounded. That's what it says on that little note, piece of paper. Now the witness says that it was on the basis of that conversation that he concluded that Mr. Stojic had authorisation and powers with respect to the entry of food and the humanitarian convoy linked to food supplies. It is beyond all logic that at a meeting -- that he links up the 31st of August meeting with the convoy of the 25th of August. It was a food convoy which entered East Mostar. Quite obviously the witness is not telling the truth here before us, because he's drawing conclusions from impossible situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: There is a more serious problem than that if I may say so. Yesterday -- this is a witness who has been tendered under Rule 92 ter, and yesterday in response to questions from the Prosecutor said that he had read his statements and that if he were to be asked questions about the subject matters contained in those statements they would be reflected by the contents. Now he's telling us he didn't have the opportunity to read each sentence of the statement that is being tendered. Your Honour, one has to ask how much more of this statement that the Prosecution wishes to place into evidence is not reliable because the witness did not read it and is unable to confirm it. It raises a very serious issue about the propriety of offering this witness under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe there is another Defence counsel that would like to intervene. You have the document in hand, I believe. I'm all ears. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm looking at this document quickly, and I find the handwriting to be illegible, but as far as I see in relation to Mr. Thornberry and this entire document has to do with the evacuation of seriously wounded people from Nova Bila --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It has to do with talks with the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness. I'm sorry. Witness. You are not allowed to interrupt anybody here. You speak when you are asked a question and otherwise you wait, and we -- as to the Judges and everyone else, we listen to the person who has the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please wait for her to finish. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I don't know how important that is. I don't know how important that is. I mean, I've just seen the document this instant, but Nova Bila is on this document, and those who know what the situation was knew that that's where there was a hospital and seriously wounded persons who belonged to the Croatian Defence Council were at that hospital in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we shall ask Mr. Scott what his position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is clearly need for some clarification here, but at the same time I also think again there has to be a dose of reality and I feel that many people in the courtroom are running far ahead and jumping to conclusions unnecessarily and unfairly. There is nothing to indicate, there's nothing to indicate substantially at this point that the witness has been intentionally misleading and certainly not perjurious. There is apparently now a reference to two different meetings but all this jumping to conclusions about what's been said or not said and lying and all is just not fair. There's simply no basis for that kind of suggestion. As this Court has observed many times, and I think just in -- either today or yesterday, these are matters that took place some years ago. The witness has looked over at times approximately 38 pages worth of statements. I think that anyone who is intellectually honest would understand that if you read a statement you might read it three or four times and on the fourth time you might see something that you didn't see before, or something might click in your mind that you didn't see the first time you read it. I suspect that's happened to everyone in this room at various times in their lives including Your Honours. You read a document for the fourth or fifth time, I never noticed that part before. I wonder about that. So it's just simply not fair to jump to these sorts of conclusions absent very compelling evidence to the contrary, and we do not have that evidence in front of us at this time. I suggest that if the witness wants to make the notebook available, it's up to him. And I suggest, again, that we back up, take a deep breath and put this in the proper context. This is not the first time that the question of notes and notebooks have come up and many witnesses have referred to them and they have not been produced. The Chamber has not required them to be produced even though they were used and referred to by the witness, and I cite as one example, one recent example, Mr. Finlayson. The Chamber specifically ruled that his notebook did not, did not have to be turned over. So let's step back, take a deep breath and apply the rules of the Tribunal and the reality and facts, not innuendo and second guessing. That's all we have so far. Now, if the witness would like and I think it's entirely his personal choice, the Prosecution has not seen it; I think that's been made clear. It's entirely the witness's personal choice if he wants to make the notebook available. I think he can do that to all sides, and of course to the Chamber. But that would be his choice, just like any other witness, including other witnesses who have come before this Chamber. But slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, just a minute please. Mr. Scott, you are a professional lawyer. I'm a professional judge. The 92 ter Rule is designed in such a way that to avoid this kind of problem. When a witness comes to the proofing session, the Prosecution should ask him or her do you have any personal notes? Do you have them with you? If you have them with you, do you wish to show them to us? And after that when you make your presentation, you indicate to the Chamber and to all the people present that the witness does have notes, that he does not wish to disclose or discloses at the last minute so that we are not taken by surprise because he is not the first witness. Other witnesses pull out notes from their pockets or their satchels and everybody is faced with the fact. So, in professional terms, we do have a particular technique here, we ask the witness, do you have any documents and so on and so forth. Which avoids this kind of difficulty occurring. I don't know whether this has been done or not because I wasn't there. Maybe you have -- can provide us with an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is routinely done with witnesses and it was -- this witness was just seen again most recently by Mr. Spork in Mostar, in the Mostar area just some weeks ago and the documents were once again confirmed and his statements were once again confirmed and not only in the presence of Mr. Spork but also the presence of the Registry. Now, to say once again to say that the witness has read his statement and studied it further and saw something that in light of -- cross-examination does have a way of focusing the mind, and I don't think it would be surprising to anyone if a witness were to go home at the end of the day and think more about the questions that were put to him in the course of the day. That is human nature. I suspect there's not a single witness who has come to court who hasn't done that. So if the witness then thinks about it further and thinks there's some clarification that can be added, then there's nothing wrong with that. We do ask. Coming back to the question, of course we do ask. But that doesn't mean we always get everything and of course, obviously, we don't have that notebook. Now, for whatever reason - but there again let's not jump to some, oh, there's something sinister here. Unfortunately, it's for better or worse, it's not the first time, it won't be the last time in this case or other cases. Things come up. I forgot that I had this. I found this in the attic. Whatever, it happens. It happened before. It will happen again. Let's not jump to conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. I think we are in a slightly difficult situation here because we are talking about substantive and procedural matters a bit in a medley and I suggest that we first clarify the issue of whether the Chamber will receive, and the parties, this notebook. And then we will deliberate on what we'll do with it, and then in the end we will come back on the issues Mr. Scott and others have discussed. Witness, you have said already that you are prepared to let the Court have the two pages that are photocopies from your book. I now ask you, would you also be prepared to make available to us the entire notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am ready to make available to the Honourable Trial Chamber the entire notebook, but I have to point out that this notebook contains a description of events that I did not testify about, and I want that to be known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a very valid answer. Now, I want to know whether the Prosecution has any objection to this notebook being made available. I think it is not the case, but I would just like to be absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. If the witness is willing, then the Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Then the Chamber will decide whether it wants to accept it, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we will do, we shall withdraw for a few minutes to deliberate. Please stay in the courtroom. We shall be back in a few minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic has something important to say to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is important. And in view of what Mr. Murphy mentioned as a key problem, and I fully subscribe to that, Mr. Scott said we have to be intellectually honest and admit that everyone of us when we read a statement for the fourth time will find something in it that we did not see the first time. As far as I understand it, this was the Prosecution's explanation of the fact that this witness spoke differently now than in the statement that we were supposed to admit here according to Rule 92 ter. In view of the fact that the witness confirmed today something that differs from what that statement says, I believe that it would be proper to look into whether this witness is supposed to testify in accordance with Rule 92 ter at all, just as Mr. Murphy said in his remarks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but -- and I allow for translation errors because I know we constantly have to do that so I certainly allow for that possibility. Your Honour, it's not what I said. I think the correct characterisation is the witness has added something not in his previous statement, not that he has said something contrary to his previous statement. Let's again be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall withdraw for a few minutes. --- Break taken at 2.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have resumed our hearing. This is a procedure which the Bench has adopted. Witness, you will answer a series of questions on this particular document. After that, we shall give you the document which you will read in your own language so that we understand what this document contains, and then you can go and fetch your document, and we will give it to the Defence teams and the Prosecution. During the break, both parties will be able to look at the document. After the break we shall resume our hearing and either the Defence teams will wish to pursue their cross-examination, in which case if they do they will let us know, and in they don't, they will also let us know. Witness, this document of which we have seen one page is a personal document of yours. When the Prosecution, together with the investigators heard you on three occasions in July 2000, in June -- and in June, did you have the document with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The investigator who at the time was Mr. Spork, did he ask you when he conducted the interview on the 16th of May, 2000, whether you had any personal documents with you on the facts or relating to the time when you worked as an interpreter for the 41st Brigade? Did he put the question to you, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he asked me and at the time I gave him all the documents I had. However, this document was lost somewhere, mislaid. I was moving. Your Honour, I had been expelled. I lived in somebody else's apartment. I lived in seven different places. I spent lots and lots of money as a tenant, and my documentation was in 10 different places. I managed to get all these documents a few days ago only when I told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document which you discovered recently, when did you come across it again? What time of year was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Going to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five or six days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you get to The Hague, before yesterday's hearing, you met Ms. Gillett. Did you meet Ms. Gillett or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you tell her that you had found this notebook again, that you'd found it a few days ago? Did you tell her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you didn't tell her. So please look at this document which we are going to give you. As this document is written in B/C/S, could you read it out to us so that we understand what it contains. Usher, please retrieve the document from Ms. Gillett. We shall put it on the ELMO. Could you, as far as possible, read out to us what's written on this document. Read it out slowly, please, so that the interpreters can translate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It would be easier if the document that is somewhere with the Defence could also be given to the witness so that he can read normally and does not have to do gymnastic exercises. Ms. Nozica, I'm talking about the paper in your hand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now please read this out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the 31st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From the beginning. From the beginning, on top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a telephone number, Vesna Zeco's telephone number. She lived in London. This is her telephone number, 9944819071785. What is her new number? Give in order to call --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, don't read so fast, please. In the first paragraph we have the telephone number of someone who lives in London. Perhaps Mr. Murphy or Mr. Stewart will be able to identify the country code.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In London. That's Great Britain. I have a notebook where I wrote down quite a few things, and among other things there is this telephone number of this Vesna Zeco, to check her telephone number because we went to meetings in Medjugorje. So sometimes we'd had the opportunity to call elsewhere. So that's how this happened to be there. Further on: "The 31st of August, 1993. Thornberry, evacuation of seriously wounded persons/N. Bila and our people plus transfer to better places for sure. "Technical, move on and carry through. Tomorrow meeting in Medjugorje (Stojic), the 1st of September, 1993. Make possible realisation, list of persons/wounded. Cakan. This is Alija Alikadic. 40 to 50 wounded persons for evacuation, children. So, Cakan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, read this slowly, please. Please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Start again with Cakan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "40 to 50 wounded persons for evacuation, women, children, adults. Dr. Milavic aware of cases. Outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. Opinion. "Dr. Milavic, 50 persons at minimum. We have no vehicles. We are seeking assistance from UNPROFOR. Destination. "Thornberry, tomorrow at meeting in Medjugorje in the morning. Meeting in Sarajevo, agreement general joint committee with UN to reach agreement. "Dr. Milavic, number of people and final site of evacuation and vehicles for evacuation. "Thornberry, five children three go to MASH," I think that's an American hospital, "Zagreb and two to Germany or as it says up here American medical field hospital, AMFH. "Dr. Milavic, aid in medicaments. 80 per cent of the medicaments are not for use. "Sally Baker, role in terms of working for non-governmental organisation. Thursday operation of transferring the wounded. SpaBat and" -- I cannot read this. "Organs of UNPROFOR. Transport." I think that this is Humo: "One, treatment of civilians, prisoners, attack by HVO every time it comes. "Thornberry, one cease-fire conditions laid by the HVO. Two, use of civilians for military targets. Three, list of persons - wounded. "Thornberry, medical assessment. So this is doctor's opinion. Tomorrow at 11.00, a meeting on the 1st of September, 1993. That's the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You just read this document. I thank you for this. But the impression we get is the following: When you're writing names, you know, Thornberry and two dots. The sentence that comes right after "Thornberry," does it mean that these are the words that he actually said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So all the people mentioned on this sheet said what you actually wrote down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's how I always take notes, as people speak, as much as I can jot down during meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So back to Mr. Stojic. In what you just said, there is no mention of the fact that Mr. Stojic will attend the meeting of September 1st. Where is this mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's mentioned right at the beginning. Mr. Thornberry -- Mr. Thornberry you have under the date the 31st of August, 1993, in the first paragraph. And in the second paragraph it says: "Tomorrow, meeting in Medjugorje," and then in brackets it says, "Stojic," and then it says, "01993, will make it possible to implement everything."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the way the sentence is written, it can be interpreted in two ways, either that Mr. Stojic will be at the meeting or that Mr. Stojic will be the person that will make all this possible. There are two options here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, in the binder for the witness we do have a document referring to all this. It was provided by the Prosecutor. It's P4857 and refers to both of these meetings. I believe the Prosecutor would have got to this but he didn't. We've moved ahead because the witness has now moved on to events that the Prosecutor has not asked questions about, but it's stated quite clearly why this meeting was held, who was there, what they said, and so on. The document is P04857.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I don't have the document that Ms. Nozica is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well -- so before the break and before the witness fetches his document and shows it to everyone. Ms. Gillett, what do you have to say on this item.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Regarding the item that Ms. Nozica just mentioned, I was about to get to that exhibit. I have another few questions before I would get to that exhibit, but it's on the Prosecution's exhibit list. Sorry, Your Honour, I don't follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you have any questions in connection to the document that was just read, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour I don't have questions with the document that was just read. I think there was a misunderstanding. I perhaps misunderstood what Your Honour was asking me. I was responding to the witness having a copy in the bundle of the document that Ms. Nozica just referred to, not to do with the document he's just read. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So if I understood you, Ms. Gillett, regarding the meeting of August 31st and September 1st, the topic is closed and you want to move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I, in the first place, wasn't dealing with anything to do with the 31st of August or the 1st of September. My questions were regarding a meeting on the 24th of August, 1993 and the issue has become confused and developed into this witness now producing notes regarding a meeting that I had not heard of before this afternoon. So my questions regarding the 24th of August have not yet finished, no. There are still some uncertainties and inconsistencies I need to clear up, and then some substantive matters that I hope to eventually get to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I think we'll have a 20-minute break first. Mr. Witness, you will go get your notebook with the usher. You will give it to the usher. The usher will then turn it over to Defence and to Prosecution. During the 20-minute break, both parties can look at it, and then we'll know what your positions are, as we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the break the document was photocopied and distributed to everyone. It is a 27-page document. It is a handwritten document. Before giving the floor to the parties, I note that as of September 1st, 1993, at that date there's mention of a meeting where obviously the person hand-wrote Briquemont, Morales and a name that I cannot decipher. I think I decipher Petkovic also, Delic. This is what we can read on the document. However, I see no mention of Stojic. This document, as such, cannot be used by Judges who do not read B/C/S. So we do not know yet whether the document will be useful or not. Can we know exactly what is the position of the Defence as of now? Ms. Nozica, you looked at the document. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have the document in the binder together with its translation into English, but by your leave this document is quite important and we will deal with it in our cross-examination depending on the witness's further replies during the direct examination. However, there are two points I wish to make. We have now received the photocopy of this notebook handed over by the witness, and the first thing I have to say is that when we look at the original of the notebook, I don't know where it is at present, in whose hands, we see that this is in fact a part of a notebook that there were many pages in that notebook, and that some pages have been torn out, the pages the witness gave when he first spoke to the OTP. The first of the pages that we have received bear the date the 25th of August, 1993. For the sake of the record, I have to say that it's rather odd that the witness was not in possession of this notebook when he provided the first part which the Prosecutor received and disclosed to us because these are evidently pages that preceded those pages of the notebook that the witness supplied today. The witness provided those pages referring to the talks of the 24th of August, 1993, and the first page that we see from the notebook today bears the next date, the 25th of August, 1993. I don't know to what extent this portion of the notebook can be useful for the Defence as a whole, but on behalf of Mr. Stojic's Defence, and I don't know whether the other Defence teams will support me, I propose that the Prosecutor continue the direct examination but that the cross-examination be postponed, that it be delayed, because we have a new situation now. We don't have the 92 ter statement because the witness has departed from it substantially, so we will need time for additional preparation for cross-examination to deal with the new elements provided by the witness today. Therefore, I propose that my learned friend continue her examination. It would be much better for all of us were it to be concluded today, and that the cross-examination of the witness be postponed because the Defence of Mr. Stojic at least will not be ready to begin the cross-examination without checking all the statements made in this notebook and the new statements made by the witness today during his examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence, please. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Now, if I understood Ms. Nozica, she has indicated that it's her belief that what was provided to us before through the Prosecution came from the same notebook, and if that is indeed the case then obviously it would contradict the gentleman's statement today. I don't know, but perhaps that's something that the gentleman could -- could answer. He's shaking his head. I assume that this is from another notebook. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask him the question, Mr. Karnavas. Witness, please, I think you heard what Ms. Nozica said. According to her, before August 25, 1993, which is the first sheet in this notebook, there must have been other pages that you handed to Mr. Spork, and you didn't hand this one and the rest. Is this what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is a notebook containing all the pages it had from beginning to end. It's a separate notebook which I found, as I told the Court. The -- whatever else I had I handed over to Mr. Spork. This is the original notebook. There are no pages torn out. It follows a logical sequence. Everything else I have handed over to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could look at the notebook one more time. If I could have the assistance of the usher. The gentleman has it with him, the original notebook, not that I don't take him at his word, but I just like to look at it myself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It would appear that no pages are missing from this particular notebook, so -- in any event.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I am correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bench would like to see it too. Ms. Nozica wants to see it also. Obviously she spoke without having seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While Ms. Nozica is looking at the notebook, I would -- first of all, we need to look at this more thoroughly over the course of the night. We are prepared to going forward with our cross-examination. So barring something that's in there that's something that needs to be explored we will be ready to continue tomorrow assuming the Prosecution finishes their direct. We don't know what their position is, whether they're going to need time. If that is the case, in any event, we think that since the gentleman is under oath that they are not to have any contact with the gentleman with respect to the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as the Petkovic Defence is concerned, we completely support what our learned friends and particularly Ms. Nozica said. Obviously, Your Honours are considering the position on the notebook, but the present situation we're in does make it most unsatisfactory to proceed with cross-examination immediately after the conclusion of examination-in-chief, and the course proposed by Ms. Nozica is the obviously sensible course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with the proposal of my colleague, Mr. Stewart. Of course we have to read this and check it. At first glance, and really at first glance, it does seem to me that we might continue with our planned cross-examination, but I will look at this later tonight and by tomorrow I will know whether it contains anything new. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I support what my colleague Ms. Nozica said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I always have reservations when notes of any kind are to be used, but that's my personal standpoint. There's something else I wish to raise. In the Hadzihasanovic/Kubura case we had a similar situation. I will not mention the name of the witness because the witness testified in closed session. The witness had a diary that he brought with him and it contained some observations of his. At that time you allowed the Defence to retain the right, after studying the diary, to recall the witness if need be and cross-examine concerning the contents of the diary. Of course it's in your hands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I wish to clarify one point. When I said that we wished the cross-examination to be postponed, I wasn't basing my request only on the notes in the diary but on the changes introduced by the witness into his statement and the introduction of new elements that the witness did not mention before when making the 92 ter statement, and that would also make it possible for us to study this diary in detail and carefully so as not to miss anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will give the floor to the Prosecution, but first I sum up what has just been said and the Defence can check this. Part of the counsels believe that they could proceed with the cross-examination as of tomorrow since there's only 27 pages to this document, some of which are irrelevant. And, for example, when I see the page where there's the name of the deputies in the Italian Assembly, I don't see what the relevance can be here. So there are probably interesting pages and others that are totally irrelevant. So part of Defence counsels believe that they could start cross-examination as of tomorrow, but other counsels believe that it would be best to postpone to a later date the cross-examination for two reasons. First because of this new document, and second, because the witness differed slightly in his testimony from what he said in the statement. So I believe that these are the two options that the Bench is confronted with when it -- before deliberating. But we'd like first to hear Mr. Scott. Maybe he will provide us with a third option.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I wish I could, Your Honour. It seems to me, as I said to Ms. Gillett a few minutes ago, it's kind of the old saying, if you're in for a penny, you're in for a pound. And given this situation, the Prosecution should not be put at a disadvantage by not having the ability to know what's in the document more than anyone else in the courtroom. Therefore, I see no alternative but to call the examination on all sides to an end. The witness will have to come back on a future occasion after the document's been translated. But most of the Prosecution, certainly those sitting here do not work -- regrettably do not work and write in B/C/S and we would have to translate and study the document and it would be completely unfair to put us to a disadvantage more than anyone else. So I guess we're at an end and the witness will have to be rescheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be heard for a second. They have staff. They have staff that translate. We're talking about a rather small document. Certainly they can do it overnight, and they can certainly continue with the planned direct examination right now and then if need be, they can go into areas which are in the document tomorrow, but I don't see the sense of wasting the rest of the week. I'm just being practical about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that -- Mr. Stewart, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is one of those occasions and perhaps it does emphasise the point that we are dealing with six Defences here. This is one of those occasions on which this Defence team does take a different stance from the position of the Prlic Defence team, and it's perhaps important for Your Honours to appreciate that from time to time, both in our private discussions but also in court, that this does happen, because we each represent our own individual clients. And the Petkovic Defence position is, Your Honour, in the light of what Mr. Scott says, it would be fair then to call the examination to a halt completely. And if the Prosecution feel conscientiously and professionally that they are faced with a similar difficulty, whether they're less or more, we needn't debate, some similar difficulty to the difficulty we're in, then we certainly wouldn't resist that. So there's that difference, Your Honour. It's bound to happen once in awhile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps, ladies and gentlemen, one could have an intermediate solution. That would be the following one: The Prosecution continues direct but will not finish direct. We postpone cross-examination but also reserve some time for the Prosecution to complete direct examination in view of the new situation. I think that could be regarded as fair to all. I wonder what the Prosecution thinks about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for being creative. I'm afraid that doesn't really help us because, I mean, speaking for Ms. Gillett, and really for the -- what is the sense of possibly putting questions to the witness which -- which will then, having been studying the document, to be shown by the document that the questions are not well put? It's professionally embarrassing, and inappropriate. So as I said, Your Honour, look, this has developed. The Defence have insisted on this. And as I said, if you're in for a penny, you're in for a pound. So if we're going to do it, we're going to do it the right way. And it will be translated and we will have a chance to study the document and go forward. And not to divide it up. We have to finish now, but they get to come back later. No, we don't agree could that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas was first, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, I fully agree with the proposal put forward by Judge Trechsel. I think it's quite logical in this situation, and we must not forget a very important point. The witness here is being heard under Rule 92 ter. The Prosecutor should continue examining the witness about the circumstances contained in the statement, and if new circumstances arise, if new information has been obtained, let the Prosecutor question the witness about them. Were the witness a viva voce witness, then Mr. Scott's proposal would be quite reasonable, but as they wanted to put in a 92 ter statement, let them complete their examination according to that rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to state the following, that I regret very much even now in the Bench we have not yet the opportunity to deliberate on that issue before and then to -- to speak about our options and about our proposals. So therefore I would like to urge ourselves and the Presiding Judge to deliberate on that question and not to rush to the conclusion, because I believe that unless the Defence teams are not -- are ready to continue, then I see a great number of strong arguments in Mr. Scott's statement, and there I believe that we have to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. But before you deliberate, Your Honours, if I may also be heard. First and foremost, I agree with Judge Trechsel's proposal for the following reason: One, as was pointed out by Ms. Nozica, this is a 92 ter. The Prosecution has met with this witness on several occasions. Now, whatever's contained in the notes that we received from the gentleman, either will provide further information that will be helpful to the Prosecution, or it may have information that may be -- they may find themselves in the regrettable position of having to impeach their own witness or it may be that there's nothing really in the notes other than some phone numbers and some innocuous notes of meetings but nothing necessarily terribly important. They have planned a direct examination, and we're trying to save time and we're trying to move forward. So I find it rather ironic that it is the Defence trying to urge the Prosecution to put on their case as they're required to do so. Now, they came here prepared. They should ask the questions. And Judge Trechsel did allow for the possibility for them to supplement, to supplement, and therefore I -- you know, I would think, I would think that they would welcome that opportunity. So -- and of course, the Defence is not going to be put at an advantage because, again, should the Prosecution wish to supplement their direct, we will be hearing it fresh and we will need to react right on the spot. So I don't see what the problem is, and I frankly find it difficult that the Prosecution is fighting at this point, having met with the gentleman for so many times, having their investigator write the statement for the gentleman, incorporating their documents into the statement and making it appear as if the gentleman was giving the narration. So now I find it ironic, supremely ironic indeed, that they're here fighting to delay the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is absurd. Once again, it's very interesting to listen to this discussion and how it shifted in the course of the afternoon. About an hour ago, it was critically important that this document be turned over. It was critically important that the document be made available to everyone, and there was great noise being made from this side about how important it was. It was a disadvantage not to have the document and et cetera. Now, when the disadvantage comes on the Prosecution's side, it's all very different, it's all very different. Now, that's just completely unfair. It's completely, absolutely unfair. It's Mr. Karnavas not being noble. He's just simply saying, we'll put the Prosecution to a disadvantage. We'll have more time. We'll do -- all of us counsel who speak and work in B/C/S can certainly go home and read this tonight and be prepared to deal with it. Sure they can. Let's have a chance to put the Prosecution at a disadvantage. It is fundamentally unfair. And it's interesting again how the dynamics have shifted from what they were an hour ago until now. It's fundamental fairness. And it's -- this very document -- it's like the suggestion now is the Prosecution can go forward. The document's not that important. Well, if it's not that important why did we just spend the last hour and a half debating about it, and taking the time? You're in for a penny, you're in for a pound. The Prosecution wants to be treated fairly, to have a chance to study the document, translate the document and then go forward. And that's where we are and we do not agree to any other proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to reassure my colleague Judge Prandler we shall withdraw to deliberate, and so far we have taken no decision whatsoever. We shall withdraw for a few minutes and will return in a few minutes and let you know what the Bench has decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber has deliberated on the matter. The Trial Chamber felt that the Prosecution wanted the document to be translated into English to be able to continue with its examination-in-chief. The Trial Chamber acknowledge the position of Defence counsel. Some wish to have more time to prepare their cross-examination, and some were prepared to cross-examine as of tomorrow onwards. Bearing in mind all of this, the Trial Chamber has decided to postpone sine die the testimony of this witness who will be called again by the Witness and Victims Unit to come to testify in the future again. The Trial Chamber will by then have a translation of the document, an English translation, which will be provided by CLSS, the translation services of the Tribunal. On a personal note, I should like to make a remark, and I shall give the floor to my colleagues if they so wish. On a personal note, in the future to avoid this kind of situation occurring again, I would like to ask the Prosecution, when it is proofing its witnesses, to automatically check with their witnesses whether the latter have any documents with them. If the witness does have any documents, make sure that you look at these documents and make sure that you let the Defence -- that you let them know about this so that this situation does not occur again. In certain cases, the witnesses don't say anything and don't say to the Prosecution, in my shoes or in my socks or in my satchel I don't have any documents, and this is something that comes up during the hearing. But if the Prosecution automatically puts the question to its witnesses then this problem would not arise. So much for this. I would also like to let the witness know that you will be asked to come again, but as you are now -- but as you have taken the solemn declaration, you are a witness of the Chamber, and you are no longer a Prosecution witness and you are not to contact the Prosecution and you are not to contact the Defence teams and you are not to contact the Bench either. So you are going to go back home, and you should expect to come back again in the near future. Also, as far as the time allotment is concerned, we will see what the Prosecution has to tell us once the document has been translated. I don't know if my colleagues wish to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I want to make the observation, but it's not on a personal line but quite objective. Having looked at this document, I cannot help noticing that there is certainly at least one piece of paper missing. Of course I cannot say whether it was torn out after the document was written and contained words or whether it was thrown out because there was some mis -- miswriting or whatever. Probably when we have a translation of the text we will perhaps see that something is obviously missing or that something is not missing. Witness, are you -- can you remember that you have torn a page, maybe an empty page, out of this -- of this piece of -- of paper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Witness. Before answering this question, what I have realised is quite different from what my colleague has just said, and this is objective. We -- we have here a sheet of paper which is still part of the notepad but could easily be torn off, but it's practically loose, and I don't see that a piece of paper has been torn out. On the second page there's a piece missing. It has been cut here. So that is what you can see. There is a sheet of paper, and number two -- the sheet of paper number two has been torn off or part of it has been torn off but there's nothing missing before that. Witness, on the face of the varying positions of the Judges, what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Book which I have. Over the past few days I did not take anything out of it. Perhaps when I was writing it I used a piece of clean paper that I needed for some other note-taking. So that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of my colleagues would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I regret that we have wasted our time today. I'm not criticising anyone here, but this is my question: I'm wondering that as far as the advice provided by the Presiding Chamber to the Prosecution is concerned and the notes taken by the witness, I'm wondering whether in the future the parties should not work together more closely, like gentlemen, and to check whether there are any notes around rather than always raising this issue before the Chamber at the last minute, which means that we have to adjourn or postpone. This is just a remark I wanted to share with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Kovacic. Just -- I would like to add something to what I said previously. I did say that as far as the sheet of paper that might have been torn off is concerned, I did say that the first sheet of paper is part of the notepad as it should be, but when you turn the first page you realise that on the second page part of the page has been torn off. But if you look at it closely, if you look between the two sheets of paper closely, you see that a sheet of paper has been taken out, which may tally with what the witness said, that a piece of paper might have been taken out. So this document will be given an IC number. Registrar, please. I shall give you the original, and please provide us with an IC number. Just a minute we need to have the IC number and then you can have the floor, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this diary will become Exhibit IC 603, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, might we have a look at the original perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem whatsoever. Usher, could you kindly give this document to the accused. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to avoid any misunderstandings or additional discussion and debate, the proposal that His Honour Judge Mindua just made, I'd like to address that. I don't know how far the Chamber knows this - and I'm sure the Prosecution will confirm it - the Defence regularly, as soon as we receive a proofing chart and the materials and documents, well, we take out the documents that have been disclosed to us, we look through them, and as soon as we see the witness mentions a notebook or a document that hasn't been disclosed, we always react straight away and send a letter to the Prosecution. That is regular practice, and that's what we do. It usually happens on a -- between Friday and Saturday. And I think we do this on a regular basis. We always react. The Prosecution always responds. They say, Yes, we do have it; no, we don't; we can disclose; we cannot. So I want to assure you that this gentlemanly communication that was referred to without doubt exists. But this is a different matter, a question here where the witness told nobody anything. Bearing in mind your ruling, Your Honour, I didn't want to raise this issue earlier on, but since you've decided to interrupt the cross-examination at this point, I would like to propose the Trial Chamber consider another issue. The whole sense of the institutional mechanism under 92 ter has been lost in this case, and if I might be allowed to paraphrase the rationale between 92 ter without entering into the whole history of how the rule came about in the first place, this rationale is that we introduce a statement, present the statement, and it must be, I would like to say, a clear statement dealing with a particular event, not the kind of statement that this witness proffered. But I don't want to go into that now. So 92 ter means you have a witness statement. You have the witness appear in court where he confirms that that is indeed his statement and that he stands by it. And the third stage is to give the Defence and opportunity to challenge the statement through cross-examination and possibly to put forward its own documents through the witness. Now, at the beginning, Your Honours, you limited 92 ter witnesses in that way, providing instructions and guidelines to the Prosecution. That was how we worked. Now we're faced with a situation like this for the first time, where we have an altered 92 ter. We have not one statement but several statements which are very -- cover a broad area. Then we, once again, have a very broad direct examination, examination-in-chief, which contributes to the scope of the statement, and we saw that in part it is contradictory to the statement. We might hear more; we might not. And then we have the cross-examination as the third segment of the story. Now, I consider that the admission of the statement, which comes at the end of this whole process pursuant to 92 ter, in its spirit, will not be in conformity with Rule 92 ter if we proceed along those lines. That is why I'd like to move this issue straight away without waiting for the next time we meet to give the Prosecution food for thought. Perhaps they will change their approach. And secondly, I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber to think about this: When the witness appears a second time, whether he can be treated as being a 92 ter witness, and it is my modest opinion that that would not be proper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did ride a different horse from Mr. Karnavas earlier, but I'm going to ride the same horse as Mr. Kovacic this afternoon on this point. I'd maybe just add - I don't want to reiterate what he said, which I support - but one of the problems about 92 ter and the way it's applied is that, in our submission, 92 ter is saying that the Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement. It contemplates that a discrete part should be admitted at times, if not the whole statement, and there may be other parts of the statement which are inappropriate to be admitted. The problem that we have is that the practice has developed where instead of - and I hope this comes across in whatever translations/interpretations ensue - that instead of statements being admitted in part, they're admitted partly, so the whole statement is admitted but it isn't the 92 ter statement. It's not the complete in-chief evidence that we have to deal with. So summarising, really, without wishing to repeat what Mr. Kovacic says, we don't know where we are because we're faced, apparently, with a 92 ter statement but in fact we get this untidy, very difficult combination of 92 ter with supplementary oral and sometimes the supplementary oral goes on for a long time. It's extremely difficult to prepare. It's extremely difficult to avoid, with all the goodwill in the world - and I regard my lead counsel as the perfect English gentleman, apart from the obvious fact that she's a Croat lady - we all try to be gentlemanly and lady-like in dealing with these matters and we are cooperative. But that situation faces us all. The Defence is faced, no doubt, with a quite impossible situation in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not an -- this is not an issue about 92 ter. The same issues would have -- if this had been a viva voce witness and the same exact thing would have happened, of course the viva voce testimony may have come out, information may have come out, that there was a notebook that had been turned over before and we would have been in exactly - exactly - the same situation. So this is not -- this has nothing to do with whether it's 92 ter or viva voce. Point number one: A completely false issue. Number two, just so the record is clear and I can provide the -- I can pull out the correspondence, if necessary, what was said to the Defence last week and what was said to the Chamber is, again, that this would be a mixed viva voce 92/92 ter witness. If everyone wants to be accurate - and I'll bring my letter next time we come to court if we need to - but I'm sure it said exactly that: Some would be 92 ter; some would be viva voce. Now, I know from talking to other Prosecution teams, Your Honour, that in other Chambers, the 92 ter procedure seems to work quite well, seems to be quite productive. I don't know why it's only in this Chamber, apparently, that it doesn't seem to work.
