I don't know why that is, but hopefully we can still get it figured out before the case is -- before the trial is over. It is a situation -- it is simply a situation, as I have said before, where you have a statement and some of it can come in in writing and some parts of it can be taken viva voce. And it's a mystery to me why that becomes so complicated. There are certain paragraphs of the statement which the Prosecution does not think require additional time. It's on crime base areas that perhaps there's been an abundance of evidence on. We don't want to present any more evidence on that particular point, so we put it in writing. There are other paragraphs that are more important, may talk about some of the accused. We take it viva voce. There's no mystery about it and it works perfectly well in other Chambers. So, again, I don't know why in this particular Chamber it doesn't seem to work as well as it should. Your Honour, again, let's come back to reality. I think some -- I get the impression sometimes, listening to some of the comments that have been made, that trials and evidence-taking and evidence collection somehow takes place in laboratory conditions, which it does not. We're talking about gathering material that's been in various places. The witness told us very direct and was easy to understand: Some of these documents have been spread all over the countryside as he was expelled from his home, and he's only just recently been able to collect some of them just days ago - just days ago - but that's a perfectly understandable answer. It's no different with a viva voce witness. Again, it wouldn't have mattered. If it was a viva voce witness, the situation would be exactly the same. And you know, sometimes viva voce witnesses, in my experience over the last 30 years, they might have remembered something different when they're on the stand that they didn't say before. And when they go home and they're in Mostar a week from now, they'll think of something, I wish I had said that because now I remember something I forgot. Boy, I wish when I was in The Hague, I wish I would have remembered that because that would have been really important. This is human -- we're dealing with human situations here. None of this takes place in laboratory conditions. And I hear some of the comments that are being made and it's just nonsense, absolute nonsense. I hope that the Rule -- in terms of Rule 92 ter, it is a productive rule and practice that I think should be usable. I don't know why, again, it seems to be so difficult in this particular courtroom, but hopefully we can get it sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like an opportunity just briefly to answer that, because I do have some experience of quite a long trial in which -- it wasn't 92 ter, but it's basically the same idea, 92 bis, the same operation in the Krajisnik trial. Now, Your Honour, I'm going far from dewy-eyed about the Krajisnik trial. At the time we made many submissions in the course of that trial as to what the Defence said was unfair and Mr. Krajisnik is appealing. So I want to leave that alone. It's not some long lost model of a trial that I'm putting forward. But in relation to this matter, the difference was this, on the use of 92 bis which now embraces 92 ter for practical purposes, that limited supplemental questioning was generally permitted by the Prosecution just to explain some of the things, which on examination of the statement really are too bare if they're just left as the written statement. That's very different from the Prosecution identifying -- and this is how I understand it, identifying particularly important paragraphs, and then having the opportunity to develop those fully in oral examination-in-chief, because I think we have to remind yourselves, notwithstanding the human nature which we all accept and Mr. Scott refers to, that 92 ter (A)(iii) requires the condition that the witness attests that the written statement or transcript accurately reflects that witness's declaration and what the witness would say if examined. And when the witness turns up because he's being cross-examined under 92 ter, when the witness turns up, that's what he is to say. Now, of course we accept that in the course of proofing of a witness with a long statement - and this is where, of course, human nature and the real world comes in - of course there are going to be some modifications and changes. That's natural. That has been allowed, as far as I'm aware, in any trial where this procedure is adopted. No Defence is going to have a problem with that. But what's happened here, Your Honour - and Mr. Scott talks as if it's got nothing to do with the Prosecution - the Prosecution, to a considerable extent, makes the choice to do this. They have the opportunity rigorously to stick to 92 ter, with those mild modifications that I've indicated, and make sure that the statement they wish to adduce under 92 ter - they always try 92 bis in the first place, but we end up usually under 92 ter - that that statement does represent for all practical purposes the evidence in-chief that we know we are going to have to meet and we are going to have to cross-examine on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be briefly heard, Your Honour. The problem with this particular witness was the statement and that's why I started yesterday by raising the way the statement was constructed. It wasn't the gentleman's statement. They met with him on three different occasions. On one of those occasions he provided the Prosecution investigator with several documents. They then came back on 10 July 2000. The contents of the documents were put in and injected into the statement as if the gentleman had given a narration, narrating what was in the document and putting somewhat of a spin on it. Now, that is not a statement. That is Mr. Spork's statement. That's what -- and then they say that they read it to him in B/C/S, of course. The gentleman can read it in English and could have read it in English and should have read it in English. There was no need for them to read it back to him in B/C/S to see whether it was accurate. But what I'm trying to suggest is that in this particular case, it wasn't the gentleman's statement; it was the investigator's statement. And by trying to do 92 ter with this particular witness, they're trying to have it both ways. And what we have -- the problem that we have in this particular courtroom is because the Trial Chamber is rather strict with the time it allows the Defence for cross-examination purposes. This statement, part and parcel of it are all the documents contained either in the statement or attached to it. In addition, they want to have virtually a full-blown cross-examination and introduce perhaps other documents. And then we have limited time for cross-examination. I think that the practice has become such that the Prosecution has two bites at the apple. They want the entire statement and then at times on direct examination they go into areas that are not necessarily part of the statement. And I would suggest that if they have another witness such as this person, with a statement that was constructed and devised and designed by their own investigator, that perhaps they simply take viva voce testimony and keep it clean, and that's the end of the story. And I don't think that I'm misstating anything. Yes, he's going to come up with some new stuff. We found out that he had notes. But as Your Honour pointed out, had they asked him, "Do you have any other notes" when he first arrived, we wouldn't be in this situation. And I'm rather surprised that Mr. Spork didn't ask him, given that the gentleman seemed to be showing up with all sorts of documents. And I find it rather ironic, because when I was reading it some light bulbs were going off. I found it ironic that the gentleman just happened to have access to certain documents in his private archive, certain copies, unsigned copies, but yet he couldn't find his own notebook that he supposedly found several days ago, at least that's what he wants us to believe. I don't know, and we haven't asked the gentleman, when was the last time he moved, because he claims that somehow it's not until 2007 that he finally got his own place and was able to relocate his possessions. And I dare say that back in 2000 he had access to documents, he had access to notes, he had access to his notebooks, because he gave them to Mr. Spork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Karnavas, that the witness can be asked when he comes back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we haven't heard you for a long time. It's a bit exceptional, so I will now give you the floor. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Well, I could meddle into all these matters with the witness and so on. I'd just like to say a few words about this little booklet. I counted that 11 pages have been torn out. I think there might be more. But anyway, it could be confirmed -- you could compare it to the outside of the book, the cover, and then you could count how thick it was and how many pages it had if you look at the binding. But at least 11 pages are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really do hate to waste time, but just one detail referring to my learned friend of the Prosecution. He touched upon the question of comparing the live testimony with 92 ter testimony. There is just one difference which my colleague seems to forget persistently. When we have live testimony, although the Trial Chamber does receive witness statements beforehand for them to be able to better follow the testimony of the witness, the statement does not become an exhibit. That's the vital difference. So what we hear in court from the witness is what is recorded in the transcript and what becomes evidence. That is the essential difference. So if I can use the word "pure" in relation to 92 ter, pure 92 ter when the rationale of 92 ter is used and when the witness speaks of one single event, and I asked -- I inquired about this with my colleagues who are dealing with the amendments to the rule, it is when one event is addressed. "They burnt my house" or "I saw when so-and-so did such-and-such in a village." Then the statement is tendered and admitted, but the witness is brought on -- in for the Defence to be able to cross-examine that piece of evidence. So you can't compare classical testimony, viva voce testimony, and 92 ter testimony. 92 ter testimony was taken by all Trial Chambers very warily because there are always additions and conditions which, with the development of this institution which is new, I have to admit, in this court, in this Tribunal, compared to other legislation and so on and practice, the Trial Chambers were very cautious in approaching. And I know that you were very cautious, too, and always acted cautiously. So we must be very wary when dealing with 92 ter. We cannot have 92 ter used or the mechanisms of 92 ter used with witnesses such as this one here, who addresses a series of events which I might say are a very important events and then even mentions some of the accused. That is just not a good example for 92 ter. And we aren't finding our way here. The Defence teams don't seem to find our way when we're given 92 ter because we base the cross-examination on the basis of his statement, because the statement becomes an exhibit and is admitted. So then I challenge that. Whereas I get a whole new block of issues in this specific case and we have to challenge that, too. And it's difficult to differentiate afterwards and make the proper analysis of what is the same and what was different. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to add something to answer Mr. Scott. 92 ter procedure is -- the interpretation given by Prosecution is not my interpretation of it. I was at the Plenary Assembly of the Judges who adopted this procedure. Article 92 ter is for witnesses that make statements that are very straightforward, and it's for statements that require no additional question. The only question to be asked is: Do you confirm what you said in your statement, period. And to my mind, I must say that you shouldn't even allow for documents being admitted in this respect. But it's true that Chambers have taken different paths, and you have invented, and you said so yourself, a new procedure. It's a mixed procedure, mixed viva voce and 92 ter, which we can't make heads or tails of anymore. I think that this comes from the Prosecution. And as Judges, the Bench notes that there are problems when the witness is answering questions, and we notice that there is a problem then. I'm sure that you'll answer, Mr. Scott, and I'll give you the floor, but I think that this is very relevant, because on page 12 of the witness's written statement, I noted that he mentions that the Croatian army was present in August 1993. And this, if the statement is admitted, could be used by the Judges in the judgement itself. Maybe Defence won't have to cross on this, because Prosecution will have said nothing. But when a 92 ter statement is admitted, it is admitted from line 1 to the very last line. You admit everything in the statement. And because of this, the Defence has to read it completely. So as a conclusion, I agree with what's been said, but I note that the 92 ter procedure here in this Chamber has taken a turn that is not in keeping with its spirit. Mr. Scott, what do you have to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are we having a seminar here? We have a witness who is sitting here and we're talking above his head. I think this is not very desirable. Could we dismiss the witness perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as you see, there's a divergence between Judges. I don't think we need the witness here because we're talking procedure. Sir, as I said, you will now leave the courtroom, and you will come back when -- at a later date, a date that will be given by the section of -- the witnesses and victims section. Unless Mr. Murphy has to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so that we can avoid any -- any further waste of time when the witness comes back, would the Trial Chamber inquire from him whether there are any other relevant documents that he has and has not given to the Prosecution so that we don't have to go through this hopefully a second time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. So, Witness, when you come back, if you come back with new binders or folders you found in one of the apartments you left, tell us. So do you have any other documents identical to the one we just saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for the moment I don't have any documents. So I won't be presenting anything else to this Court. Not in my possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if you by chance run into another of these notebooks, do you undertake to disclose it immediately through the Victims and Witnesses Section to the party involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I will now ask the court usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, on Article 92 ter with all the observations made, could you tell us the position of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'll try to be very brief. To be perfectly honest I'm of half a mind not to say anything further because I'm sure that once I say something then somebody else will be up and it's never-ending but be that as it may, some very specific things have been said towards the Prosecution so I think it's only fair that the Prosecution at least give a brief response to those things. I want to assure the Chamber that the Prosecution routinely asks witnesses if they have materials. The Chamber shouldn't presume incompetence or negligence on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, and we routinely do ask that question. That doesn't prevent situations from arising just as we've seen today and as I said about an hour and a half ago, it's happened before and it'll happen again. And one of the Defence counsel, just a few minutes ago, indicated it happened in another case. And we don't work in a perfect system and we never will, but I can assure the Chamber and let me say it again very, very clearly, we routinely ask witnesses those questions. So it's not something that we never thought of before, number one. Number two, as I said sometime previously, 92 ter was not -- not created by the Prosecution. It was adopted by the Judges in Plenary Session and the Judges have said that you're about to have a Plenary this afternoon. The Judges of this Tribunal came together and adopted that rule, and they adopted that rule, as an efficiency measure - let's be very honest about it - because this Tribunal doesn't have enough time to conduct all of its proceedings in a different way. If you did, you wouldn't have limited the Prosecution to 293 hours to present its case. So the institution cannot have it both ways. You cannot limit our ability to present our case and then use the slowest possible methods for us to do so. And I don't direct that just to this Chamber, I direct it to the institution as a whole. You can't say, "You only have 293 hours to present your case, and by the way, not only that, we're going to make you do it in the slowest possible way." And it was the Judges of this Tribunal, sitting in Plenary Session, who adopted Rules like 92 bis and 92 ter - not the Prosecution, the Judges - to attempt to address these situations. And the use of it in a mixed way is not unique to this Prosecution team but has been done in other Chambers routinely. And I've talked to my colleagues, I've talked to the other STAs in all the other cases, and it's not something that's invented by this Prosecution team. I don't see anything in the rule -- when I look at 92 ter (A), I don't see anything in the rule that says something about it can only be used with straightforward witnesses. I don't see that language in the rule anywhere. What I do see is that a Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement, and that's what the Prosecution has tried to do. It doesn't limit the Defence's ability to go into their cross-examination on both the -- if there is viva voce parts or on the 92 ter statement. Indeed, if it was viva voce, what do you think they would cross-examine on in part? The prior statement. So even if it was a viva voce witness, what would they go to to cross-examine the witness? The statements. What would they be complaining about of the Prosecution if we went out beyond the scope of the statements? "Your Honour, that wasn't in the statement." So, again, Your Honour, a lot of things are being said this afternoon that just really do not stand up to scrutiny. I wish we had more time to go through every one of the things that have been said in that regard. 92 ter is a procedure that I think could be productive. It could help everyone. I don't know if the Defence plans on using it in their case or not. Perhaps they won't use it. Perhaps they'll feel that they have more than adequate time to present their case without using such tools as that. But I don't think it's the Prosecution being unfair and I don't -- I take exception to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave. In respect of time and how we are going to use the time, we certainly share this concern with the Prosecutor. Of course everyone is thinking in terms of how to use the time available in the best possible way. I just want to say that in the chart that we received for this witness, it says that he would be heard viva voce and that his direct examination will be three and a half hours. So even had he been heard viva voce, nothing would have been controversial. Now, what is the controversy? What the Prosecutor wanted now. According to 92 ter, he wanted to introduce the statement. That is the only thing that we challenge. Let's not forget where the problem arose today. Not on account of the diary. That just happened by the by. At one point in time the witness had a piece of paper. All of us in this courtroom noticed that he had a piece of paper, whereas the witness who made this statement looked at it. He said yesterday that his statement was fully accurate. Today he was giving a completely different story with regard to a very important matter. And then he said that last night he saw that there was a mistake in what he had said. That is where the problem is with 92 ter. There is one thing that he says viva voce and there is another thing he says in his statement. That is where the problem is, not on account of the diary. That kind of mistake can always be made. However, the problem here is that the statement is being brought into evidence, along with a full viva voce testimony. So fully in terms of the time that this witness was given, he basically gave a viva voce statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is what it looks like from our point of view: The witness says just one thing, say, about electricity. He went to Croatia, and then in order to explain who it was that was giving electricity to whom, a lot of papers have to be prepared. He mentioned Gacice and I heard the witness mention over 40 different theses. So in order to refute these theses on water supply, power supply, and so on, about the Croatian army, there is an abundance of documents involved. So how can we refute that? What I did in the SDA party, so on and so forth, five or six minutes are required at minimum to question him. So now we have to prove our innocence and we don't have enough time. That's what I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So there's been a debate on 92 ter. Next week a witness is scheduled. The Prosecution requested seven hours, and it is a witness that will be heard for four days. We're already halfway through June. Mr. Scott, I asked you last time for a schedule giving the time that you have left and, according to our decision confirmed by the Appeals Chamber, which is interesting, we would like to know the Prosecution's schedule before the end of the Prosecution's case. So either you cannot produce it, which I understand, or you're producing it or you haven't started producing this schedule. But the Judges, the Bench, would like know exactly what is in store, to know where we're going. Mr. Scott, could you give us some information on this general schedule for all witnesses to come?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First off, Your Honour, I have to say I will continue to look at it in light of today's discussion. But we anticipate that next week's witness would also be a mixed 92 ter/viva voce witness. Let me just say that now so there's no mistake about that. As to the larger -- as to the broader schedule, Your Honour, we're look -- we're actually actively looking at that. It involves a number of decision. It involves a number of factors about what evidence is coming in as we go and what evidence we will not -- we will forego. I can absolutely assure the Chamber that we're looking at it very actively. I don't think - I have to say, I have to say in fairness, I don't think that it ultimately matters a whole lot in terms of whether you see that next week or a month from now. The Prosecution is going to present its case, the case the Prosecution wants to present, and we will present it until the last hour; and if it runs out at 293 hours, then we'll be finished. So we'll continue to go forward, selecting the witnesses that we think are the best ones that we want to present in the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a problem with that response. While I respect the Prosecution's right to put on its case and to choose its witnesses and its documents and to do so at its pace, nonetheless the Trial Chamber has also indicated, based on looking at the initial witness list that the Prosecution had presented way back when it had 400 hours that it had decided not to call certain witnesses, and the Trial Chamber had indicated that it may wish to call some of those witnesses at some point. And we all know, based on the rules, that the point normally comes at the end of the trial. Now, again - again - my concern is as follows: The Defence, because the Prosecution has the burden of proof, first of all, the Defence is only -- if, indeed, we end up putting on a defence, it will be based on the Prosecution's case. That's why we need to know which witnesses it will call. We also will need to know which witnesses the Trial Chamber may wish to be called -- wish to call at the end of the trial, because it's unfair to the Defence to, one, try to -- if it does put on a defence to meet the Prosecution's case and then the Trial Chamber comes back and calls Prosecution witnesses, albeit it will be court witnesses, but nonetheless these were witnesses that the Prosecution intended to call. And let's face it, the only reason that the Trial Chamber would be aware of many of these witnesses is because of the 65 ter and the summaries that was presented by the Prosecution. So I do think that it is relevant and it's important to the Trial Chamber to have, as expeditiously as possible, the Prosecution's list. It should have at least within -- within some flexibility, they should know more or less who are they going to call, especially when it comes to important expert witnesses and what have you. That would then allow the Trial Chamber to perhaps give us a judicial hint, which is quite normal in the German system to get judicial hints from the Bench, and perhaps at that point we may be suggesting to the Trial Chamber to provide the Prosecution with some additional time to put on its full case if the Trial Chamber insists on hearing from certain witnesses. That way we can then make a decision if indeed we need to put on a case, and, if so, we can put on a case based on the Prosecution's case. So I do take exception with Mr. Scott's position that it doesn't make a difference and they'll proceed as they wish. I think the Court issued an order; they need to live up to that order. And if they don't wish to abide by it, they should be very clear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, first off, Your Honour, since it's been raised several times this afternoon - and I said I would do it if necessary and I want to be consistent and a man of my word - this is a letter that was sent to the Defence on the 1st of June and I read it, quote, and we can put it on the ELMO and everyone can read it, if necessary. It says: "Although we intend to call this witness as a 92 ter/viva voce witness, we disclose this additional material as part of full disclosure." So if anyone doubts my word, there it is. I'll be happy to provide it to the Chamber if anyone thinks I'm not reading it correctly, number one. On the issue of schedule, Your Honour -- I don't know about judicial hints. We don't get judicial hints where I come from. But if the Chamber wants to clue me in on some of the Chamber's thinking, I'll be happy to receive it. Your Honour, the Defence have made -- at least some of the Defence have made a big issue of the fact that they think any court witnesses will be called at the end of the case after all parties have presented their evidence. If that's the case, if that's the case, then it makes no difference whatsoever whether we tell you which witnesses we're not going to call next week or we tell you that in October, because you will not make the decisions on which witnesses you're going to call a year and a half from now until then. And whether we tell you tomorrow or we tell you in two months, it will make no difference as to when you get that information as to when you're going to call those witnesses at the end of the case. Once again, it's a complete disconnect with what's being said. We certainly have an idea. We indicated in a filing we made with the Chamber some weeks ago that a large number of witnesses had been, whatever you want to say, put aside, would not be called, and we listed all -- we listed all those. We also listed a number that would be called and we also indicated a middle category of people who we were still looking at, and we are still doing that. But I have to -- with all respect to the Chamber, with utmost respect to the Chamber, I have to say again: The Prosecution will present its case. It may not be the Chamber's case. The Chamber might want to call other witnesses, but the Prosecution will present its case until it concludes its evidence. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, we don't doubt Mr. Scott's word but of course we don't always agree with it. There's a difference. Secondly, although I defer to Mr. Karnavas's knowledge of the German legal system, we do often receive hints where I come from. Sometimes they're subtle; sometimes they smack you between the eyes. So all information is gratefully received, Your Honours. Thirdly, just to put down a marker and certainly not to wish to open up a seminar about Chamber witnesses this afternoon, there is something inherently odd about the notion that we might get to the end of the Prosecution case and then the Prosecution are not given time to call witnesses that they would regard as necessary and yet the Trial Chamber takes the time to call the same witnesses. But, Your Honour, perhaps that's a -- perhaps that's a matter that we, on the Defence side, should talk about, because Mr. Karnavas has raised a point about Chamber witnesses, I've raised just that marker point about Chamber witnesses. It's not a straightforward issue, Your Honour. So the invitation there is - I think we made it before a couple of weeks ago, really - is to invite, respectfully, the Trial Chamber to proceed cautiously and to give all parties a full opportunity of making full representations on all these matters relating to Chamber witnesses before any final decisions are taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I agree with what Mr. Stewart has said just for one technical reason that I think I've raised before, but it is one that's very important. At the close of the Prosecution case, we have the opportunity of making a motion under Rule 98 bis, and the terms of that rule are very specific, that the Trial Chamber has to consider whether a motion to dismiss certain counts should be granted based on the Prosecution's case, and we will be submitting that what that means is the case presented by the Prosecution as distinct from any additional evidence that the Trial Chamber may at a later time feel, if the case goes that far, the Trial Chamber may -- may feel the need to supplement it. But we would strongly urge that at the time when the Prosecution's case is over, that would be the appropriate place to make our motion under Rule 98 bis. So I think it does have a bearing on the timing of any possible further evidence after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's reciprocal support between Mr. Murphy and me on these issues because what he's said is not in the least inconsistent with what I said, nor is it intended to be and we fully support the observation he's just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, as far as the Chamber witnesses are concerned, I said this last time, we have not discussed this among ourselves. The Trial Chamber is unable to tell you what its position is because we have not discussed this. We have not deliberated on the matter. We don't even know where we're going since the Prosecution does not wish to give us the list of upcoming witnesses because the Prosecution feels that that is their responsibility. So we are unable to let you know. We hope we will be informed of the upcoming witnesses. As Mr. Murphy has said at the end of the Prosecution case the Defence will file its oral motion pursuant to Rule 98 bis, and the Trial Chamber will determine the matter pursuant to the oral motion and information provided by the Prosecution. After that, the trial comes to a halt if an acquittal is granted. If, on the other hand, pursuant to Rule 98 bis the trial will continue, a reasonable trier of fact should be informed of any additional material. So that you are as familiar with this procedure as we are. So we expect to get this list. Let me turn to the Prosecution and say that we have already cut down on time, and if I come to notice that we are wasting a lot of time, I may ask the Bench to reduce the time even more. It is now 10 minutes past 5.00. In a few moments, the Judges will have to go and attend the Plenary Session. As we have no more witnesses for this week, we shall reconvene and meet again on Monday at a quarter past 2.00, which will allow both parties to get on with your job because you have a lot of work to do. The Court stands adjourned.
